pairs.rationale: Both accounts introduce John preaching in the wilderness; Mark also describes his baptism as a baptism of repentance.
Luke likewise places John in the wilderness and then describes his proclamation around the Jordan; Matthew specifies the wilderness of Judea.
John's announcement here and Jesus' announcement in Matthew 4:17 both call for repentance because the kingdom of the heavens has drawn near. The speakers and occasions differ.
Matthew explicitly identifies Isaiah as the source of the wilderness voice preparing the Lord's way and making His paths straight; Isaiah's wording names the paths of our God.
Both Evangelists use Isaiah's wilderness-voice passage to explain John's ministry and quote the commands to prepare the Lord's way and straighten His paths.
Both descriptions give John's camel-hair clothing, leather belt, and diet of locusts and wild honey.

John's leather belt recalls the description by which the king identifies Elijah. The texts differ in their description of hair: Matthew specifies camel-hair clothing, whereas 2 Kings calls Elijah a hairy man; this is a proposed Elijah association rather than an identical costume quotation.
Both accounts describe people from Jerusalem and Judea going out to John; Matthew additionally names the region around the Jordan.
Both accounts state that John baptized people in the Jordan River while they confessed their sins.
Both record John's address 'Brood of vipers' and his question about fleeing the coming wrath. Matthew identifies Pharisees and Sadducees among the arrivals, whereas Luke addresses the crowds.
Both versions of John's warning require fruit worthy of repentance; Luke continues in the same verse with the warning against relying on Abrahamic ancestry.
Both reject the boast that Abraham is the hearers' father and state that God can raise children for Abraham from stones.
Both versions place the axe already at the trees' root and warn that a tree without good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire.

Both contrast John's water baptism with the stronger coming One's baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire. John's unworthiness is expressed through carrying sandals in Matthew and untying the sandal strap in Luke.

Mark also records John's announcement of a stronger successor, his unworthiness concerning the successor's sandals, and the contrast between water baptism and Holy Spirit baptism. Mark's cited passage does not include Matthew's reference to fire.
Both describe the coming One clearing His threshing floor, gathering wheat into His storehouse, and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire.
Both accounts bring Jesus from Galilee to John for baptism in the Jordan; Mark specifies Nazareth as His Galilean point of departure.
Luke also records Jesus' baptism in the context of the people's baptism, adding that He was praying when heaven opened; Matthew describes His arrival to be baptized by John.

Matthew presents John's sense of being subordinate to Jesus through his objection that he needs Jesus' baptism; John presents the baptizer's confessed unworthiness to untie the coming One's sandal. John does not repeat the baptismal objection.

Both baptism accounts describe Jesus coming up from the water, heaven opening, and the Spirit descending like a dove. Matthew says the Spirit came upon Him, whereas Mark says into Him in this edition.

John's testimony describes the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon Jesus; Matthew narrates the corresponding descent at Jesus' baptism. John's testimony also explains the sign's identifying purpose.
Both accounts record a heavenly voice declaring Jesus the beloved Son in whom God is well pleased. Matthew presents the declaration in the third person and Mark as direct address to Jesus.
Luke likewise places the heavenly declaration of beloved sonship and divine delight at Jesus' baptism, together with the Spirit's dove-like descent.
Both accounts place Jesus under the Spirit's leading in the wilderness and identify the devil as the one testing Him; Luke specifies the forty-day duration in the second verse.
Mark likewise joins the Spirit's action in sending Jesus into the wilderness with His temptation by Satan; Mark says the Spirit drove Him out.
Both describe Jesus abstaining from food for forty days and becoming hungry afterward; Matthew additionally specifies forty nights.
Both record the devil challenging Jesus' divine sonship by asking Him to turn stone into bread; Matthew uses plural stones and loaves, while Luke uses singular stone and bread.
Jesus' answer cites Deuteronomy's contrast between living by bread alone and living by every word from God's mouth. Deuteronomy places the saying in Israel's experience of hunger and manna.

Luke also records Jesus answering the bread temptation with the written saying that a human being does not live on bread alone. Luke's quoted wording in this edition ends there, without Matthew's additional clause about every word from God.
Both accounts place Jesus on the temple's pinnacle at the devil's instigation; Luke names Jerusalem, whereas Matthew calls it the holy city. The temptation appears in a different sequence in Luke.

The tempter quotes the psalm's promise of angels commanded concerning the protected person and of hands preventing the foot from striking a stone. Matthew's citation omits the psalm's clause about guarding in all one's ways. This edition numbers the psalm 90.
Luke likewise records the challenge to divine sonship, the command to jump from the temple, and the angel-protection citation about being lifted by their hands.
Jesus counters with Deuteronomy's prohibition against putting the Lord God to the test. Deuteronomy continues by recalling Israel's testing at the place called Testing.
Both accounts give Jesus' response to the temple challenge as the prohibition against putting the Lord God to the test.

Both describe the devil showing Jesus the world's kingdoms. Matthew specifies a very high mountain and their glory; Luke describes the display as occurring in a moment of time and places it earlier in the temptation sequence.

In both accounts the devil offers the displayed kingdoms or their authority and glory in exchange for Jesus' bowing in worship. Luke additionally reports the devil's claim that their authority was handed over to him.

Jesus cites the command to worship and serve the Lord God. The Saints Deuteronomy text says to fear, serve, and cleave to Him; Matthew renders the response as worship and adds the explicit exclusivity 'Him alone.' The wordings are related without being identical.
Both accounts answer the demand for worship with the written requirement to worship the Lord God and serve Him alone; Matthew also commands Satan to go away.
Both wilderness accounts include angels ministering to Jesus. Matthew places this after the devil leaves, while Mark mentions angelic ministry within his compressed wilderness account.
Both end the temptation sequence with the devil departing. Luke specifies departure until an opportune time; the cited Luke verse does not include Matthew's angelic ministry.
Both relate Jesus' move into Galilee to John having been handed over; Matthew says Jesus heard of it and withdrew, whereas Mark introduces His Galilean proclamation.

Both locate Jesus' subsequent activity in Capernaum in Galilee. Matthew describes settling there after leaving Nazareth; Luke describes His arrival there and Sabbath teaching rather than a settlement notice.

Matthew introduces the following Isaiah citation as fulfilled through Jesus' move into the Galilean region. The cited Isaiah verses name Zebulun, Naphtali, the sea route and Galilee, then announce light for those in darkness; fulfillment is Matthew's stated interpretation.

Matthew cites Isaiah's geographical sequence of Zebulun, Naphtali, the sea route, beyond the Jordan, and Galilee of the nations. The verse is Isaiah 8:23 in this edition; its longer wording continues beyond Matthew's excerpt.

Both texts announce great light for people in darkness and light for those in the land or shadow of death. Isaiah addresses people walking in darkness, whereas Matthew describes people sitting in darkness. This edition labels the Isaiah verse 9:1.
Both summarize the start of Jesus' Galilean proclamation with the nearness of God's kingdom and a call to repent. Mark also calls for belief in the gospel and says the appointed time is fulfilled.
Both accounts show Jesus beside the Sea of Galilee seeing the brothers Simon and Andrew casting a net, and both identify them as fishermen. Matthew additionally identifies Simon as Peter.
Both record Jesus calling the fishermen to come after Him and promising to make them fishers of people or men.

Jesus' promise of fishing for people corresponds to His promise to Simon in Luke that he will catch people alive. Luke places the saying after the extraordinary catch of fish, so the comparison does not assume identical narrative circumstances.
Both describe the brothers' immediate response as leaving their nets and following Jesus.

Both identify James and John as Zebedee's sons, place them in a boat attending to their nets, and record Jesus calling them. Matthew places their father in the boat in this verse, while Mark mentions him in the response.
Both describe Zebedee's sons leaving their father in response to Jesus' call and going after Him. Mark additionally mentions hired workers in the boat.

The later Matthean summary repeats the combination of synagogue teaching, proclamation of the kingdom's good news, and healing every disease and infirmity; here the region is Galilee, while Matthew 9:35 refers to cities and villages.
Both summarize Jesus traveling throughout Galilee and proclaiming in the synagogues. Matthew adds broad healing activity; Mark's summary explicitly mentions casting out demons.

Both describe sick people being brought to Jesus, His healing varied diseases, and His dealing with demons. Luke gives an evening scene and the demons' cries; Matthew gives a wider regional summary including Syria, seizures, and paralysis, so this link compares the activity without equating the settings.

Both crowd summaries name Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, and beyond the Jordan as regions from which people followed or came to Jesus. Matthew additionally names the Decapolis; Mark additionally names Idumea and the Tyre-Sidon region. The overlapping geography does not prove a single occasion.

deferred.reason: The source verse was read. No target was retained in this batch for Jesus' specific instruction to permit His baptism to fulfill all righteousness. Matthew 21:32 calls John's ministry a way of righteousness and Matthew 5:17 describes Jesus fulfilling the Law and Prophets, but neither explains this distinctive baptismal exchange closely enough to count a completed pair here. Further substantive review remains pending.

review_notes: Read all 42 source units in Matthew chapters 3 and 4 in the saved Saints text. No source wording changes were proposed.
Retained targets were read directly in the Saints reference cache. Quotation wording differences were stated rather than silently harmonized.
Preserved Greek-based target numbering: Psalms 90:11–12; Isaiah 8:23 and 9:1. Isaiah 8:23–9:1 is one ordered cross-chapter target passage for the fulfillment introduction at Matthew 4:14.
The temptation sequence differs between Matthew and Luke. Angelic ministry in Mark's compressed account is not assigned Matthew's exact temporal placement.

Matthew 3:14 to John 1:26–27, Matthew 4:19 to Luke 5:10, and the regional crowd/healing comparisons are thematic parallels with their limitations stated; they do not claim an identical recorded exchange or occasion.
Matthew 3:15 remains deferred with zero completion credit. The Matthew 21:32 and 5:17 candidates were read but rejected for this batch as insufficiently specific.
